newsitem.title: UK: Dollar/mark scales new peaks as traders test Buba.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/mark scales new peaks as traders test Buba.

text.p: The dollar vaulted to near-eight- year highs against the mark on Monday as traders threw down the gauntlet to the Bundesbank, challenging it to follow up its threat to raise key money-market rates to stem the mark's slide.

Expectations that German growth is too weak to withstand sustained rate rises, as well as recent evidence of the strength of U.S. growth, propelled the dollar above 1.87 marks for the first time since October 1989.
"The market is taking the Bundesbank on and looking to force its hand," said Mark Geddes, treasury economist at ABN Amro.
"The Bundesbank has got to be able to do a number of moves but the question is how credible is such a move when domestic demand is relatively weak."
The dollar, which rose as high as 1.8705 marks by midsession Europe, was at 1.8686/96 at 1030 GMT from 1.8631/36 late Friday in Europe.

While the dollar also hit new peaks against other European currencies like the Swiss franc and the Italian lira, it made less headway against the yen. Expectations Japan will protest against dollar gains above 120 yen and talk of higher Japanese interest rates hampered the dollar's progress against the yen.

The U.S. currency reached a four-year high of 1.5350 Swiss francs and hit 1828.35 Italian lire, the strongest it has been in more than a decade. Dollar/yen, meanwhile, was at 118.55/60, little changed from 118.37/47 on Friday.

The dollar has surged more than 14 percent against the mark since early February, when Germany and other members of the Group of Seven leading industrial nations called for an end to its two-year rebound.
The mark has also slumped against other major and European currencies, tumbling to its weakest in five years in trade-weighted terms, analysts at ABN Amro said.
This has prompted the Bundesbank in recent weeks to foster talk that it could use variable-rate tenders to nudge its securities repurchase rate up from a record low of 3.0 percent.

For one, it has fixed the repo rate for two weeks rather than the full four-week duration of its summer recess. Traders also said Germany may also turn to its G7 partners for support if the mark keeps weakening against the dollar.
"The Germans can't be too happy with these three-big-figure moves every week," said a currency trader in London. "I think the G7 will try to protect the 1.90 level, at the very least by talking."
"If you were long from downstairs that is okay, but I would be nervous of re-establishing long positions up here."

While such caution may slow the dollar's rise in the coming days, analysts such as Rob Hayward, economic adviser at Bank of America, do not expect the dollar to dawdle for long below 1.90 marks as long as economic fundamentals are in its favour.
"German data should show that it will be difficult for the Bundesbank to raise rates," Hayward said.
By contrast, U.S. data on Friday, including a stronger-than-expected July jobs report, "painted a very positive picture of the U.S. economy."

Such expectations were little changed by a report which showed German industrial output rose 1.4 percent in June, even though the German Economics Ministry said the increase was likely to be revised up substantially.
Analysts are therefore expecting traders to test the limits of German and G7 endurance in the coming weeks.
"People are keen to buy on dips and dollar/mark is going to 1.90," said Geddes at ABN Amro.
